source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025, v3) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (RaM)
finding: Direct use of the Value of Computation idea (the machine form of expected value of control). Reward = correctness minus a token cost; trained with expert iteration so the model reasons only when it pays.
numbers: Abstract: 23-45% fewer tokens than few-shot CoT and STaR across three models, accuracy kept or raised. Table 1 Llama-3.1-8B: STaR 47.4% acc / 222.7 output tokens; RaM 50.1% / 170.8. Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct: STaR 61.9% / 215.1; RaM 63.5% / 146.2. Few-shot direct answer 33.5-45.8% with 0 output tokens.
quote: Our method trains LLMs to use intermediate reasoning steps selectively when they are likely to be beneficial.
limits: Training needed (not a prompt). Small open models (Llama 3.2-3B, 3.1-8B). Accuracy is rescaled. Datasets are mostly reasoning-light except GSM8K and Proofwriter. Earlier version (v1) reported 38%; later versions report 23-45%.
agent_relevance: S0 and G11/G12 have a formal basis: pay for thinking only when expected gain beats token cost. A scaffold can mimic it with a cheap pre-check, but the trained form is not available to us.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025, v3) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (RaM)
finding: Does the model adapt, or just reason less? Items were split into easy (direct answer already right) and hard. RaM widens the gap in chain length between hard and easy items; the instruction-tuned CoT model did not adapt length to difficulty.
numbers: Length reduction on easy vs hard up to 50.3% on Llama-3.2-3B; RaM spends 23-32% fewer tokens than STaR on average.
limits: Difficulty defined by whether the direct answer was correct, so it is a proxy for need, not a measured payoff.
agent_relevance: Gives a testable measure for an S0 gate: does thinking length track need? The same easy/hard split can audit our scaffold.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025, v3) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (RaM)
finding: Out-of-distribution transfer and boundary: on MMLU-CF the learned policy cuts tokens, but one model lost accuracy, and savings are smaller on subjects that need multi-step reasoning (physics, engineering).
numbers: MMLU-CF, Llama-3.2-3B: STaR 27.0% acc / 150.6 tokens vs RaM 29.5% / 96.3. Llama-3.1-8B: STaR 40.2% / 153.6 vs RaM 36.4% / 110.6 (accuracy fell 3.8 points). 28-36% fewer tokens than STaR.
limits: Partial failure of free savings: the cost term can undershoot on a model that is weaker out of distribution.
agent_relevance: Savings are not free. Keep a floor on thinking for multi-step classes.

source: De Sabbata, Sumers, AlKhamissi, Bosselut, Griffiths (2025, v3) Rational Metareasoning for Large Language Models (RaM)
finding: The paper cross-checks its result against a meta-analysis (Sprague et al 2024): chains help mainly on maths or logic and bring marginal gains elsewhere. Its own results agree.
numbers: Cites a meta-analysis of over 100 papers.
limits: Secondary citation inside the paper.
agent_relevance: The expected benefit of thinking depends on task class, so S0 should route by class.

source: Oh and Gobet (2025) Monitor-Generate-Verify (MGV): Formalising Metacognitive Theory for Language Model Reasoning
finding: Theory paper. Writes the EVOC explicitly for LLM agents: EVOC(b,c) = Q*(b,c) = E[r(b,c) + V*(B_t+1) | b,c]; optimal control picks the argmax. Adds a Monitor step before generation. Describes the Learned Value of Control (LVOC) as a feature-weighted approximation learned from experience.
numbers: No experiments. Cites a 'prefix dominance trap' with nearly 20% accuracy loss when a suboptimal strategy is chosen early (Luo et al 2025, not opened).
quote: Though we present no empirical validation, MGV provides a vocabulary for diagnosing component-level failures
limits: Authors state there is no empirical validation. The 20% figure is second-hand.
agent_relevance: Supports a monitor step at S0 (judge difficulty and confidence before generating). Treat as design vocabulary, not evidence.

source: Zhou et al (2026) When More Thinking Hurts: Overthinking in LLM Test-Time Compute Scaling
finding: Marginal utility of extra thinking tokens falls and then turns negative. Correct answers flip to wrong at long budgets. Optimal length depends on difficulty, so uniform allocation wastes compute.
numbers: AIME 2024+2025 (60 problems), R1-32B: +3.2% per 500 tokens early; accuracy 37.8% at 2K, 46.5% at 4K, 53.8% at 8K, 55.8% at 12K (peak), 54.9% at 16K (12K to 16K: -0.9 points, 95% CI -1.4 to -0.4). s1-32B peak 47.6% at 12K. Flip ratio (wrong flips / right flips) first exceeds 1 at 7K tokens (1.09, p=0.038); at 8K CI 1.21-1.68. s1 crosses at 5K.
limits: Budget forcing on two 32B models; math and GPQA only; 60 problems is small. Of 80 hand-checked negative flips, 67.5% were genuine overthinking and 12.5% other types.
agent_relevance: The payoff curve of thinking is concave then falling. This is the marginal side of EVOC: stop when marginal gain per token drops below cost. Cap near the knee.

source: Zhou et al (2026) When More Thinking Hurts (difficulty and stopping)
finding: Difficulty moves the optimum: easy MATH-500 problems peak near 1.5K tokens, hard (Level 5) keep gaining up to about 8K. GPQA Diamond shows the same pattern, peak near 10K. Indicator-based early stopping (log-prob and trace features) predicts negative flips.
numbers: Easy (Level 1-2) peak 1.5K; Level 5 peak 8K; GPQA peak 10K; combined indicators 76.3% precision at 80% recall for predicting negative flips.
limits: Indicators tuned on the same model families; no external replication. Authors say effects may differ outside math and science.
agent_relevance: Gives numbers for G12 (budget per difficulty) and a cheap stopping signal for S0 and later loops.

source: Zhai et al (2026) Adaptive Test-Time Compute Allocation for Reasoning LLMs via Constrained Policy Optimization
finding: Formal EVOC for compute: per input pick budget b maximising Acc(x,b) minus lambda times cost(b), lambda a shadow price; average cost is monotone in lambda, so one price hits any budget. A small classifier learns the rule from cheap text features.
numbers: MATH, 200 questions, 3 seeds, at average budget 3.0, gain over fixed budget: +5.8 points (DeepSeek-V3), +5.2 (GPT-4o-mini), +6.4 (Qwen2.5-7B). DeepSeek-V3 MATH: fixed 0.517, learned 0.575, oracle 0.586. Abstract: up to 12.8% relative gain, over 91% imitation accuracy of the oracle.
quote: closed-form oracle action that optimally prices accuracy against cost
limits: Only 200 questions per set and a small menu of budgets. GSM8K (about 94.6% base) gains are tiny (0.946 to 0.965) because there is little to reallocate.
agent_relevance: Cleanest machine analogue of the payoff-minus-cost rule. Needs per-item accuracy curves offline; our scaffold can approximate with a difficulty guess and a price.

source: Snell, Lee, Xu, Kumar (2024) Scaling LLM Test-Time Compute Optimally can be More Effective than Scaling Model Parameters
finding: Best way to spend test-time compute depends on prompt difficulty. A compute-optimal policy that picks the strategy per difficulty bin beats uniform best-of-N.
numbers: About 4x less test-time compute than best-of-N for the same result (e.g. 16 vs 64 generations). FLOPs-matched against a 14x larger model: test-time compute wins on easy and intermediate questions, not on the hardest. Beam search helps hard questions; on easy ones it hurts (verifier over-optimised).
limits: PaLM 2-S* on MATH; difficulty is estimated from model pass rate, and predicted-difficulty bins lose part of the gain vs oracle bins.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G12 and for allocating by difficulty. The estimated-difficulty gap is the honest limit of any S0 gate.

source: Chen et al (2025) Do NOT Think That Much for 2+3=? On the Overthinking of o1-Like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend huge effort on trivial items with no gain. The first solution is usually already right.
numbers: For '2 plus 3', 1,953% more tokens than conventional models; 13 solutions generated. In over 92% of cases the first round of solutions gave the correct answer. Self-training that removes redundant rounds cut QwQ-32B-Preview output by 48.6% on MATH500 at kept accuracy.
quote: In more than 92% of cases, the initial round of solutions produces the correct answer.
limits: QwQ-32B-Preview, a research preview; tested on GSM8K, MATH500, GPQA, AIME. Pruned by self-training, not by a live cost rule.
agent_relevance: Failure case of a missing EVOC gate: no effort cost in the model's own control. Stop after the first sound solution on easy items.

source: Aggarwal and Welleck (2025) L1: Controlling How Long A Reasoning Model Thinks With Reinforcement Learning
finding: Length can be set in the prompt, giving a dial for control intensity (the 'how strongly' axis of EVOC). Smooth accuracy-versus-tokens trade-off; short reasoning models emerge.
numbers: Beats S1 by up to 100% relative and 20% absolute on math under equal conditions; 100-150% relative and 20-25 points absolute at 512 and 1024 token budgets. 1.5B L1 at equal length beats GPT-4o. L1-Exact about 1% below its unconstrained base.
limits: 1.5B model trained by RL; S1 truncates mid-thought, so part of the gap is a weak baseline. SelfBudgeter reports L1 collapses on AIME2025.
agent_relevance: Intensity is controllable by instruction. A scaffold that sets a token cap per item has a machine-readable knob.

source: Li et al (2025) SelfBudgeter: Adaptive Token Allocation for Efficient LLM Reasoning
finding: Model first states a token budget from the query, then reasons within it. Reward: correct answers peak at a minimal sufficient length; wrong answers push for longer. Users see the cost before it is paid.
numbers: Average length compression 61% on math at kept accuracy. 1.5B: GSM8K +11.01 accuracy points at 43% of length; MATH500 +3.54 points at 44%; AIME2025 30% of length, accuracy comparable. 7B: average 48% compression. Ablation: format reward alone collapses accuracy (GSM8K 1.64%).
limits: DeepSeek-R1-Distill 1.5B and 7B; RL training. Authors say L1 fails on AIME2025 and E1 hard truncation hurts accuracy.
agent_relevance: A pre-stated budget is an EVOC-like commitment. The pre-budget step can be done by prompt: predict cost first, then decide whether to go on.

source: Arora and Zanette (2025) Training Language Models to Reason Efficiently
finding: RL with a length penalty (one hyperparameter) gives a family of cost-sensitive models. Savings are larger on easy problems.
numbers: 7B model: tokens -16% on AIME 2024 (accuracy -3.3 points), -37% on MATH500 (-2.2), -65% on GSM8K (-1.7). At alpha 0.2: 27% savings on AIME, 83% on GSM8K.
limits: R1-Distill 1.5B and 7B; small accuracy losses everywhere, so cost is not free; training required.
agent_relevance: Confirms the shape of the optimal rule: spend less where easy. The price parameter is the lambda of EVOC.

source: Sprague et al (2024) To CoT or not to CoT? Chain-of-thought helps mainly on math and symbolic reasoning
finding: Meta-analysis of over 100 papers plus own runs on 20 datasets and 14 models. CoT gains are large on math and formal logic and small elsewhere. On MMLU, direct answers match CoT unless the question or answer contains an equals sign.
numbers: 100+ papers; 20 datasets; 14 models. Non-symbolic categories (commonsense, reading comprehension, knowledge) show little separation; paired bootstrap with Bonferroni correction on 13 datasets.
quote: CoT can be applied selectively, maintaining performance while saving inference costs.
limits: Prompt-based CoT only; long-horizon planning not covered; contamination not controlled.
agent_relevance: Rule for the S0 gate: expected value of thinking is high for symbolic or multi-step items and near zero for knowledge or commonsense items, so answer plainly there (G11).

source: Liu et al (2025) Mind Your Step (by Step): Chain-of-Thought can Reduce Performance on Tasks where Thinking Makes Humans Worse
finding: Human psychology predicts where deliberation hurts; the same holds for models in three of six task types: implicit statistical learning, verbal overshadowing in face recognition, learning labels with exceptions. The payoff of control can be negative.
numbers: o1-preview vs GPT-4o on implicit statistical learning: -36.3 points absolute. CoT lowered accuracy in all 6 vision-language models on face recognition. Learning with exceptions: up to 331% more iterations. The other three archetypes gave mixed results.
quote: CoT reduces performance...up to 36.3% absolute accuracy for OpenAI o1-preview compared to GPT-4o
limits: Models and humans do not share processes; only 3 of 6 predicted effects held.
agent_relevance: Negative value of control is real: on perceptual or pattern tasks, deliberation can lose. S0 must be able to choose 'do not think'.

source: Srivastava et al (2025) LLMThinkBench: Do LLMs overthink basic math reasoning?
finding: Benchmark of 14 basic math tasks over 53 LLMs. Reasoning models use far more tokens and sometimes do worse; accuracy collapses under tight token limits; the accuracy-verbosity curve is non-monotonic.
numbers: Reasoning models 6,780 tokens on average vs 378 for standard models (abstract: 18x more tokens). Accuracy drops from 72% to 44% at a 1,024-token limit (up to 36% drop under constraint). Quantized models keep reasoning, so overthinking comes from training.
limits: Basic arithmetic only; 'Overthinking Score' (harmonic mean of accuracy and token efficiency) is the authors' own new metric.
agent_relevance: Failure modes at both ends: overthinking easy items, and collapse when cut off. Hard cuts need a graceful fallback.

source: Zhang et al (2025) AdaptThink: Reasoning Models Can Learn When to Think
finding: Skipping thinking (NoThinking: an empty thinking block) is better for simple problems. RL teaches a reasoning model to choose Thinking or NoThinking by difficulty. This is the 'whether' decision of EVOC.
numbers: On three math datasets, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: average response length -53%, accuracy +2.4%.
quote: AdaptThink reduces the average response length of DeepSeek-R1-DistillQwen-1.5B by 53% and improves its accuracy by 2.4%
limits: Training required; math only; the NoThinking claim comes from Ma et al 2025, restated here. Author list not checked.
agent_relevance: Strongest direct evidence for a binary S0 gate: skip thinking on simple items with no accuracy loss.

source: Aggarwal, Madaan, Yang, Mausam (2023) Let's Sample Step by Step: Adaptive-Consistency
finding: Training-free allocation: keep sampling until agreement among answers is stable (a stopping rule on the majority). Many samples are spent only when answers disagree.
numbers: 17 datasets, 3 LLMs: sample budget cut by up to 7.9 times with average accuracy drop under 0.1%. On SVAMP comparable accuracy with fewer than 5 samples per input.
quote: Adaptive-Consistency reduces sample budget by up to 7.9 times with an average accuracy drop of less than 0.1%
limits: Needs several full samples. Gains depend on how early a majority shows.
agent_relevance: Prompt-level, no training: a loop-based EVOC gate. Our S3 and S4 can stop drawing attempts once agreement is stable.

source: Li et al (2024) Escape Sky-high Cost: Early-stopping Self-Consistency (ESC)
finding: Sample in small windows and stop when a window is unanimous. A control scheme sets the cost-performance balance per task and model.
numbers: Samples saved: MATH -33.8%, GSM8K -80.1%, StrategyQA -76.8%, CommonsenseQA -78.5%, Coin Flip -84.2%, Last Letters -67.4%, comparable performance.
limits: Older models; savings vary with task (a third saved on MATH).
agent_relevance: Second training-free case. Hard tasks save least, as EVOC predicts.

source: Yang et al (2025) Dynamic Early Exit in Reasoning Models (DEER)
finding: Training-free: at reasoning transition points, force a trial answer and stop if the model is confident in it. Early exit can also improve accuracy.
numbers: 10 benchmarks, 11 reasoning LLMs: CoT length cut by 19.1% to 80.1% on average while accuracy rose 0.3% to 5.0%.
limits: Calibration of the trial answer is the weak point; ranges are wide across models.
agent_relevance: A live monitor gate that can be done by prompt: ask for a provisional answer at checkpoints and stop when confident.

source: Zhou et al (2026) Thinking Economically: Hierarchical Adaptive Budgeter (HAB)
finding: Budgets should vary at two levels: per problem and per step inside a chain. A global budget, even a learned one, ignores that step difficulty varies. HAB predicts reasoning depth, then budgets tokens by step.
numbers: Reported on GSM8K and MATH500 with Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama3.1-8B-Instruct; stronger accuracy-token trade-off than baselines. Exact table figures not extracted.
limits: Only abstract and claims read closely; two small instruct models.
agent_relevance: Suggests EVOC is needed per step, not only at S0.

source: Survey (2025) Reasoning on a Budget: A Survey of Adaptive and Controllable Test-Time Compute in LLMs
finding: Taxonomy: L1 controllability (fixed budgets) and L2 adaptiveness (scale by difficulty or confidence). Current models spend fixed compute regardless of task, overthinking easy and underthinking hard ones.
numbers: Survey with a benchmark of proprietary LLMs; no single headline number.
limits: Taxonomy only; trade-off benchmark covers few models.
agent_relevance: Map of which parts of EVOC (whether, which, how much) have machine versions.

source: de Varda, Fedorenko et al (2025) The cost of thinking is similar between large reasoning models and humans (PNAS), via MIT News
finding: Reasoning models' token counts track human response times across problem types. Arithmetic was cheapest and the ARC challenge costliest for both humans and models.
numbers: No coefficients in the news piece; the PNAS page (doi 10.1073/pnas.2520077122) returned 403, so the paper was not read.
limits: Only a press article was read. Models and sample size unknown to me. Pointer, not evidence.
agent_relevance: If it holds, token count is a fair stand-in for the effort cost in the EVOC rule.

source: Lieder, Shenhav, Musslick, Griffiths (2018) Rational metareasoning and the plasticity of cognitive control (as described in MGV)
finding: As cited by Oh and Gobet: LVOC approximates EVOC with a weighted sum of features learned from experience, so the control system predicts value instead of computing it.
numbers: The MGV reference list cites this work; I read the MGV description only.
limits: Second-hand; the 2018 paper itself was not opened.
agent_relevance: Design pattern: S0 can learn a cheap predictor of payoff from past items.

source: Gap check across the papers opened (this session)
finding: None of the papers opened ran the classic human paradigms (effort discounting, Stroop, task switching) on LLMs. LLM work tests the normative rule (value minus cost) only through token budgets.
numbers: 0 of 20 sources opened tested effort-discounting choice in LLMs. Two web searches for such studies: one found none, the second hit a quota limit.
limits: Absence of evidence after a limited search.
agent_relevance: Do not claim LLMs show human-like effort costs. What is shown: payoff-minus-cost is a workable engineering target.

source: Cross-paper check: cost terms can hurt (RaM, SelfBudgeter, Arora and Zanette)
finding: Trained cost penalties trade accuracy for tokens in places: L1 collapses on AIME2025; E1 hard truncation hurts; RaM lost 3.8 points on one model out of distribution; Arora and Zanette lost 1.7-3.3 points.
numbers: RaM Llama-3.1-8B MMLU-CF 40.2 to 36.4; Arora 7B AIME -3.3 points; L1 poor on AIME2025 (SelfBudgeter Table 1).
limits: Different benchmarks and bases.
agent_relevance: Set the cost price low on hard items. A price that is too high hurts where thinking has value.
